The Conspiracy on Titan Station

By JAMES MacCREIGH

Revolution was brewing on Titan Station, and Thomas Silva held the secret that would make the uprising succeed or fail. Yet he could make no move, could favor no side—his memory was gone—he didn't know for whom he fought.

Silva's hand flicked to his waist and hung there, poised. His plasma pistol remained holstered.

The tall, silver-haired woman—Catherine Willis—smiled.

"You're right, Silva," she said. "I could blast you, too. Nobody would win that way, so let's leave the weapons where they are."

The muscles twitched in Thomas Silva's cheeks, but his voice, when it came, was controlled. "Don't think we're going to let this go," he said. "We'll take it up with Dixon tonight. We'll see whether you can cut me out!"

The silver-haired woman's smile faded. She stepped forward, one hand bracing her against the thrust of the fusion engines underneath, holding to the guide rail at the side of the transport's corridor.

She said, "Silva, Dixon is your boss, not mine. I'm a free agent; I work for myself. When we land on Titan Station tonight I'll be with you when you turn our—shall I say, our cargo?—over to him. And I'll collect my fair share of the proceeds. That's as far as it goes. I take no orders from him."

A heavy-set man in blue appeared at the end of the connecting corridor. He was moving fast, but stopped short when he saw the two people.

"Hey!" he said. "Course correction—get to your cabins." He seemed about to walk up to them, then reconsidered and hurried off. Neither person paid any attention.

Silva said, "Do I have to kill you?" It was only a question as he asked it, without threatening.

A muted alarm bell sounded through the P.A. speakers, signaling a one-minute warning. The silver-haired woman cocked her eyebrow.

"Not at all," she said. She took the measure of her slim, dark-haired opponent. Taller, heavier, older, she was still no more uncompromisingly belligerent than Silva, standing there. "Not at all," she repeated. "Just take your fifteen thousand and let it go at that. Don't make trouble. Leave Dixon out of our private argument."

"Damn you!" Silva flared. "I was promised seventy-five thousand. I need that money. Do you think—"

"Forget what I think," Willis said, her voice clipped and angry. "I don't care about fairness, Silva, except to myself. I've done all the work on this—I've supplied the goods. My price is set, a hundred and fifty thousand Earth credits. What Dixon promised you is no concern of mine. The fact is that, after I've taken my share, there's only fifteen thousand left. That's all you get!"

Silva stared at her a long second, then nodded abruptly. "I was right the first time," he said. "I'll have to kill you!"

Already his hand was streaking toward the grip of his plasma pistol, touching it, drawing it forth. But the silver-haired woman was faster. Her arms swept up and pinioned Silva, holding him impotent.

"Don't be a fool," she grated. "Silva—"

The P.A. speaker rattled, blared something unintelligible. Neither heard it. Silva lunged forward into the taller woman's grip, sliding down to the floor. The silver-haired woman grappled furiously to keep her hold on Thomas's gun arm, but Thomas was slipping away. Belatedly, Willis went for her own weapon.

She was too late. Silva's was out and leveled at her.

"Now will you listen to reason?" Silva panted. But he halted, and the muzzle of his weapon wavered. The floor swooped and surged beneath him as the thrust of the mighty jets was cut off. Suddenly there was no gravity. The two people, locked together, floated weightlessly out to the center of the corridor.

"Course correction!" gasped silver-haired Willis. "Good God!"

The ship had reached the midpoint of its flight. The bells had sounded, warning every soul on it to take shelter, to strap themselves in their pressure bunks against the deadly stress of acceleration as the ship reversed itself and began to slow its headlong plunge into Titan Station. But the two people had not heeded.

The small steering rockets flashed briefly. The combatants were thrust bruisingly against the side of the corridor as the rocket spun lazily on its axis. The side jets flared once more to halt the spin, when the one-eighty turn was completed, and they were battered against the opposite wall, still weightless, still clinging to each other, still struggling.

Then the main-drive bellowed into life again, and the ship began to battle against its own built-up acceleration. The corridor floor rose up with blinking speed to smite them—

And the lights went out in a burst of crashing pain for Thomas Silva.

Someone was talking to him. Silva tried to force an eye open to see who it was, and failed. Something damp and clinging was all about his face, obscuring his vision. But the voice filtered in.

"Open your mouth," it said. "Please, Thomas, open your mouth. You're all right. Just swallow this."

It was a man's voice. Silva was suddenly conscious that a man's firm hand was on his shoulder. He shook his head feebly.

The voice became more insistent. "Swallow this," it said. "It's only a stimulant, to help you throw off the shock of your—accident. You're all right, otherwise."

Obediently he opened his mouth, and choked on a warm, tingly liquid. He managed to swallow it, and lay quiet as deft hands did something to his face. Suddenly light filtered through his closed eyelids, and cool air stirred against his damp face.

He opened his eyes. A slight dark-haired man in white medical uniform was standing there. He stepped back a pace, a web of wet gauze bandage in his hands, looking at him.

"Hello," he whispered. "You—where am I?"

"In the medical bay," the medic said. "You got caught out when the ship changed course. Lucky you weren't hurt, Thomas. The woman you were with—the old, silver-haired one, Willis—wasn't so lucky. She was underneath when the jets went on. Severe spinal damage—internal bleeding. She died in the other room two hours ago."

Silva screwed his eyes tight together and grimaced. When he opened them again there was alertness and clarity in them—but there was also bafflement.

"Sir," he said, "who are you? Where am I?"

"Thomas!" There was shock and hurt in the tone of his voice. "I'm—don't you know me, Thomas?"

Silva shook his head confusedly. "I don't know anything," he said. "I—I don't even know my own name."

"Silva, Silva," a man's heavy voice said. "That won't wash. Don't play dumb on me."

"Silva?" he said. "Silva...." He swiveled his head and saw a dark, squat man frowning at him. "Who are you?" Thomas asked.

The dark man laughed. "Take your time, Silva," he said easily. "You'll remember me. My name's Dixon. I've been waiting here for you to wake up. We have some business matters to discuss."

The medic, still eyeing Silva with an odd bewilderment, said: "I'll leave you alone for a moment. Don't talk too much to him, Mr. Dixon. He's still suffering from shock."

"I won't," Dixon promised, grinning. Then, as the medic left the room, the smile dropped from his face.

"You play rough, Silva," he observed. "I thought you'd have trouble with Willis. I didn't think you'd find it necessary to put her out of the way so permanently. Well, no matter. If you had to kill her, it's no skin off my nose. Give me a release on the merchandise. I've got your money here."

Silva waved a hand and pushed himself dizzily erect, swinging his legs over the side of the high cot. A sheet had been thrown over him, but he was fully dressed. He examined his clothing with interest—gray tunic, gray leather spacer's boots. It was unfamiliar.

He shook his head in further confusion, and the motion burst within his skull, throbbing hotly. He closed his eyes until it subsided, trying to force his brain to operate, to explain to him where and what he was.

He looked at the man named Dixon.

"Nobody seems to believe me," he said, "but I really don't know what's going on. Things are moving too fast for me. Really, I—why, I don't even know my own name! My head—it hurts. I can't think clearly."

Dixon straightened, turned a darkly-suspicious look on Silva. "Don't play tricks on me," he said savagely. "I haven't time for them. I won't mince words with you. Give me a release on the cargo now, before I have to get rough. This is a lot more important to me than your life is."

"Go to hell," Silva said shortly. "I'm playing no tricks."

There was an instant's doubt in Dixon's eyes, then it flashed away. He bent closer, peered at Silva. "I almost think—" he began.

Then he shook his head. "No," he said. "You're lying all right. You killed Willis to get her share—and now you're trying to hold me up. That's your last chance that just went by, Silva. From now on, I'm running this show!"

He spun around and strode to the door, thrust it open. "Hawkins!" he bellowed. "Green!"

Two large, ugly men in field-gray uniforms, emblazoned with the crossed-hammers insignia of Titan Station's Security Force, came in, looking to Dixon for instructions.

"Silva here is resisting arrest," Dixon said. "Take him along. We'll fix up the charges later."

"You can't do that," Silva said wearily. "I'm sick. If you've got something against me, save it. Wait till my head clears. I'm sure I can explain—"

"Explain, hell." The dark man laughed. "If I wait, this ship will be blasting off for Europa within two hours. I'll wait—but so will the ship. It's not going anywhere till I give it clearance. I run Titan Station; I'll give the orders here!"

II

Whoever this man Dixon was, thought Silva, he was certainly a man of importance on Titan Station. As he had said, he gave the orders.

The crew of the rocket made no objection when Dixon and his men took Silva off without a word. Silva had thought the medic, who seemed a good enough sort, might have said something on his behalf. But he was out of sight as they left. A curt sentence to a gray-clad official on the landing pad where the rocket lay, and the man nodded and hurried off, to tell the rocket's captain that the ship was being refused clearance indefinitely.

A long, powerful ground vehicle slid up before them. Dixon got in front, while the two uniformed men shoved Silva into the back of the vehicle, climbed in beside him. Dixon gave a curt order, and the vehicle shot forward.

The driver, sitting beside Dixon, leaned forward and reached a hand under the dashboard. The high wail of a siren came instantly from the vehicle's roof, and what traffic was on the broad, straight highway into which they had turned pulled aside to let them race through.

Ahead lay the tall spires of a city. Graceful, hundreds of feet high, they seemed dreamlike yet somehow oddly familiar to Silva. Somewhere he had seen them before. He dragged deep into his mind, plumbing the cloudy, impenetrable haze that had settled on it, trying to bring forth the memories that he should have had. Amnesia, they called it; complete forgetting of the happenings of a lifetime. He'd heard of it—but never dreamed it could happen to him!

My name, it seems, is Thomas Silva, he thought. And they tell me that I killed a woman!

The thought was starkly incredible to him. A silver-haired woman, it had been; someone named Willis. He tried to remember.

Yes, there had been a silver-haired woman. And there had been an argument. Something to do with money, with a shipment of goods that Willis had supplied to Silva. There had even been talk of killing....

But—murder! Silva looked at his hands helplessly.

Dixon, up ahead, was turning around. He looked sharply at Silva, for a long second. An uncertainty clouded his eyes, and abruptly he looked forward again without speaking.

"Who's this man Dixon?" Silva whispered to the nearest guard.

The man stared at him. "Administrator Dixon," he said, "is the Council's deputy on Titan Station. You know—the Earth-Mars Council. They put Administrator Dixon here to—well, to administer for them."

"Council?" Silva asked, wrinkling his brow. He had heard something about a Council once, yes. But it was all so nebulous....

The other guard stirred, leaned over. "Shut up," he said heavily. "You'll have plenty of chance for talking later."

But the chance was a long time in coming. Silva found himself, an hour later, still in the barred room into which he'd been thrust. The guards had brought him there, at Dixon's order, and left him. That had been all.

This was not a regular jail, Silva realized. It was more like a governmental complex, something reflecting the architectural design principles of Earth's brutalist period, all concrete and angular lines. Silva wished for human companionship—particularly that of the medic. Of all the people he'd met since awakening in that hospital bed, only he seemed warm and human. The others were—brutal, deadly. It was too bad, Silva reflected, that he'd failed to remember him. He'd seemed hurt, and he had certainly known him by first name. But perhaps he would understand.

Silva sat down on a lumpy, sagging bed and buried his head in his hands. Dim ghosts of memory were wandering in his mind. He tried to conjure them into stronger relief, or to exorcise them entirely.

Somewhere, some time, a woman had said to him, "Dixon is secretly arming the Titan Station dissidents for revolt against the Council. He wants personal power—he's prepared to pay any price for it. He needs weapons, Earth weapons smuggled in through the Council patrol. If he can wipe out the Security Force garrison—those who are loyal to the Council, still, instead of to Dixon—he can sit back and laugh at any fleet Earth and Mars can send. Transports are clumsy in an atmosphere. They're helpless. And if he can arm enough of Titan Station's malcontents, he can't be stopped. That's why he'll pay for plasma rifles with their weight in platinum."

Silva could remember the scene clearly. Could almost see the sharp, aquiline face of the woman who had spoken to him. But there memory stopped.

A fugitive recollection raced through his mind. He halted it, dragged it back, pinned it down....

They had stopped in Queenstown Region, the spaceport on the outer rim of the Glendale colony in Aldoria, as if the settlement knows shame and wants to hide the rough and roaring dome city that nestles in one of the great craters. Silva remembered sitting in a low-ceilinged, smoke-heavy room, across the table from a tall woman with silver hair. Willis!

"Six thousand plasma rifles," the woman had said. "Latest government issue. Never mind how I got them; they're perfect. You know my price. Take it or leave it. And it's payable the minute we touch ground on Titan Station."

There had been a few minutes of haggling over terms, then a handshake and a drink from a thin-necked flagon of pale-yellow liquid fire.

He and the silver-haired woman had gone out then, made their way by unfrequented side streets to a great windowless building. Silva remembered the white-hot stars overhead, shining piercingly through the great transparent dome that kept the air in the sealed city of Queenstown Region, as they stood at the entrance of the warehouse and spoke in low tones to the man who answered their summons.

Then, inside. And they were looking at a huge chamber full of stacked fiber boxes—containing nothing but dehydrated agricultural products and mining tools, by the stencils they bore. Silva had turned to the silver-haired woman with a puzzled question—and the woman had laughed aloud.

She dragged one of the boxes down, ripped it open with the sharp point of a handling hook. Short-barreled, flare-mouthed guns rolled out, tumbling over the floor. Ten of them were in that one box, and hundreds of boxes all about. Silva picked one up, broke it, peered into the chamber where the tiny capsule of U-235 would explode with infinite violence when the trigger was pulled, spraying radiant death four thousand yards in the direction the gun was aimed....

And that memory ended.

Silva got up, stared at his haggard face in the cracked mirror over the bed. "They say I'm a killer," he thought. "Apparently I'm a gun-runner as well. Good lord—what am I not?"

His reflection—white, drawn face made all the more pallid by the dark hair that fell over it—stared back at him. There was no answer there. If only he could remember—

"All right, Silva." The deep voice of a guard came to him as the door swung open. "Stop making eyes at yourself."

Silva looked around. The guard beckoned. "Administrator Dixon wants to speak to you—now. Let's not keep the administrator waiting."

A long, narrow room, with a long carpet leading from the entrance up to a great heavy desk—that was Dixon's office. Silva felt a click in his memory as he entered. This was a deliberate application of political philosophy and systems thinking to urban planning—one of the ancient Earth dictators had employed just such a psychological trick to overawe those who came to beg favors of him. Mussolini, or some such name.

The trick failed to work. Silva had other things on his mind; he walked the forty-foot length of the room, designed to imbue him with a sense of his own unimportance, as steadily as he'd ever walked in the open air of his home planet.

Whichever planet that was.

The guard had remained just inside the door, at attention. Dixon waved him out.

"Here I am," said Silva. "What do you want?"

Dixon said, "I've had the ship inspected and what I want is on it. That saves your life, for now. But the cargo is in your name. I could take it by force, if I had to. I prefer not to." He picked up a paper, handed it to Silva. "In spite of your behavior, you can keep alive. You can even collect the money for the guns—Willis' share as well as your own. This is a release form, authorizing my men to take six hundred and thirty cases of dehydrated foods and drilling supplies from the hold of the Meridian—the ship you came on. Sign it, and we'll forget our argument. Only, sign it now and get it over with. I'm losing patience, Silva."

Silva said, without expression, "No."

Dark red flooded into Dixon's sallow face. His jaws bunched angrily and there was a ragged thread of incomplete control to his voice as he spoke.

"I'll have your neck for this, Silva," he said softly.

Silva looked at the man's eyes. Death was behind them, peeping out. Mentally he shrugged. What difference did it make?

"Give me the pen," he said shortly.

Dixon exhaled a deep breath. You could see the tension leave him, the mottled anger fade from his face and leave it without expression. He handed the paper to Silva without a word. He gave him a pen, watched him scrawl his name.

"That," he said, "is better." He paused a moment ruminatively. "It would have been better still if you'd not stalled me so long. I find that hard to forgive in my associates."

"The money," Thomas said. If he were playing a part—pretending he knew what he was doing—he might as well play it to the hilt. "When do I get it?"

Dixon picked up the paper and looked carefully at the signature. He creased it thoughtfully, stowed it in a pocket before answering.

"Naturally," he said, "there will have to be a revision of terms. I offered a hundred and sixty-five thousand Earth-credits. I would have paid it—but you made me angry. You'll have to pay for that."

Silva said, "I've paid already. I've been dragged from pillar to post by you. That's enough. Pay me what you owe me, if you want any more of the same goods!"

That was a shot in the dark—and it missed the mark.

Dixon's eyes widened. "You amaze me, Silva," he said. He rose and stepped around the desk, confronting Silva. "I almost think you really have lost your memory, Silva," he said. "Otherwise, surely you would know that this is all the rifles I need. With them I'll take whatever else I want!"

Silva said, "You're ready, then...."

He took time to think it over, but he knew that no thought was required. Already the hands that he had locked behind him were clenched, taut. Already the muscles of his legs were tensing.

"You're ready," he repeated. "You've armed the Titan Station dissidents—the worst elements on nine planets. You're set to betray the Council that gave you power here.... Well, that changes things. I can't let you do it!"

He hurled himself at Dixon, hands sweeping around to grapple for the dark man's throat. Dixon, off-balance, staggered backward. But his own hands were diving for the twin heat guns that hung at his waist.

Silva saw his danger, and reacted. His foot twisted around Dixon's ankle; his hands at the other's throat gripped tighter. He lunged forward, slamming the hard top of his head into the other's face, feeling flesh and cartilage give as Dixon's nose mashed flat. His own head pin-wheeled dizzily, agonizingly, as the jar revived the pain of his earlier accident.

But Dixon, unconscious already, tumbled back with Silva on top of him. His head made an audible, spine-chilling thud as it hit the carpeted floor.

Silva got up, retrieving the two heat guns, and stared at him.

"They tell me I killed Willis the same way," he thought. "I'm getting in a rut!"

But Dixon was not dead, though he was out as cold as the void beyond Pluto. The thick carpeting had saved him from a broken head.

Silva stepped over the unconscious man and looked around the room. It was furnished severely, to the point of barrenness. Two chairs before Dixon's ornate, bare-topped desk and one luxurious chair behind it; a tasseled bell cord within easy reach of Dixon's chair; the long carpet. That was all it contained.

The problem of getting out was serious, he saw. How could one—

III

Methodically he ransacked the drawers of Dixon's desk. Papers, a whole arsenal of hand guns, Titan Station currency by the bale, ominously black-covered notebooks with cryptic figures littering their pages—those were the contents. A coldly impersonal desk, without the familiar trivia most men accumulate. There was nothing, certainly, that would get him out of a building that so closely resembled a fortress.

He tumbled the things back into the drawers helter-skelter, turned Dixon over and searched his pockets. More money—the man must have had a fortune within reach at all times—and a few meaningless papers. Silva took the release he had signed and tore it to shreds. But that was only a gesture. When Dixon came to, unless Silva had managed to get away and accomplish something, the mere lack of written permission would not keep him from the rocket's lethal cargo!

When Dixon came to....

An idea bloomed in Silva's brain. He looked, then, at unconscious Dixon—and the idea withered again.

He had thought of forcing Dixon himself to front for him, at gun's point, in the conventional manner of escaping prisoners. But fist fights, fiction to the contrary notwithstanding, leave marks on the men who lose them. Dixon's throat was speckled with the livid marks of Silva's fingers; Silva's head, butting Dixon in the face, had drawn a thick stream of crimson from his nostrils, turned his sharp nose askew.

No guard of Dixon's would have been deceived for an instant, looking at that face—even assuming that Dixon could have been forced to cooperate by the threat of a gun. Which, considering the stake Dixon had in this play, was doubtful....

He stood up and looked around. He had to act quickly. Already Dixon's breath was audible; he saw the man grimace and an arm flopped spasmodically on the floor. Consciousness was on its way back.

Silva touched the heat gun he'd thrust into his belt; drew it and held it poised, while he sought to discover what was in his own mind. He'd killed a woman already, they said. Was he then a killer—could he shoot Dixon now, in cold blood, with so much to gain and nothing to lose?

This was ethical decision-making at its most stark. The question of social justice weighed on him—Dixon was planning to arm dissidents who would overthrow legitimate authority, plunging Titan Station into chaos. Yet Silva found himself unable to pull the trigger on an unconscious man.

He stood there a moment. Then, abruptly, he reversed the weapon and chopped it down on Dixon's skull.

There was a sharp grunt from the still unconscious man, but no other sign. Only—the first tremors of movement that had shown on him halted, and did not reappear.

"No," Silva thought. "Whatever they say, I'm not a killer!"

But still he had to get out. How?

Once more he stared around the room, catalogued its contents. The guard would be getting impatient. Perhaps any minute he would tap the door, first timorously, then with heavier strokes.

The guard! There was a way!

Silva eyed the length of the room. Forty feet—it would take him a couple of seconds to run it at full speed. Was that fast enough?

There was only one way to find out.

He walked around the desk to the bell cord. He took a deep breath, tugged it savagely, and at once was in speedy motion, racing toward the door, his footsteps muffled in the deep, springy carpet. Almost as he reached it, he saw it begin to open. He quickly sidestepped and was out of the guard's sight, behind the door, as the man looked in.

Quick suspicion flared in his eyes, then certainty as he saw Dixon huddled on the floor. He opened his mouth to cry out—

But Silva's arm was around his throat, and he had no breath to spare. Silva's foot lashed out and the door slammed shut; Silva's balled left fist came up and connected with the guard's chin. Abruptly the man slumped.

Silva took a deep breath and let the man drop to the floor. But he paused only a second; now he had two unconscious men on his hands and he dared let neither revive until he was prepared.

He grasped the guard's arm and dragged him roughly the length of the room. He leaped on top of the desk, brutally scarring its gleaming top with the hard spikes of his boots. His agile fingers unfastened the long bell cord without causing it to ring and, bearing it, he dropped again to the floor.

Tugging and straining, he got the limp form of Dixon into his own chair, bound him with the bell cord, gagged him with the priceless Venusian-silk scarf Dixon wore knotted about his throat. He tested his bindings with full strength, and smiled. Those would hold, let Dixon struggle as he would.

The guard he stripped of clothing, bound and gagged with his own belt and spacer's kerchief. He dragged him around behind the desk, thrust him under it out of sight. Dixon's chair he turned so that the unconscious face was averted from the door. Should anyone look in, then, the fact of Dixon's unconsciousness might not be noticed.

Then he took off his own clothes, quickly assumed the field-gray uniform of the guard. It fit like the skin of a fruit. He felt himself bulging out of it in a dozen places. The long cape the guard wore would conceal that, perhaps. In any case, there was nothing better.

Trying to make his stride as martial as possible, he walked down the long carpet to the door, opened it and stepped outside.

The corridor beyond was empty, stretching in both directions with the cold efficiency of bureaucratic architecture. Silva's heart pounded as he moved forward, trying to look purposeful, trying to remember which way they had brought him in. His mind, still clouded by amnesia, offered no help.

He chose left, walking with measured steps. Two other guards passed him, nodded curtly, continued on. He forced himself not to look back, not to betray his nervousness.

At the end of the corridor, a lift. He stepped inside, studied the panel. Twenty floors, and he was on the eighteenth. He pressed the button for the ground level and felt the lift descend smoothly.

When the doors opened, he stepped out into a vast lobby. People in civilian clothes moved about, conducting business. More guards stood at various posts. And there, across the expanse of polished floor, were the main doors leading outside.

Silva walked toward them, every nerve screaming at him to run. But he maintained his pace, kept his face impassive. A guard at the door nodded to him as he approached.

"Shift change already?" the guard asked.

Silva grunted noncommittally and kept walking. The guard shrugged and let him pass.

Outside, the artificial atmosphere of Titan Station pressed around him, the great dome overhead showing the swirling orange clouds of Saturn beyond. He was free—for now.

But free to do what? He still didn't know who he really was, what side he was truly on. The weapons were still on that ship, waiting to fuel a revolution that might be just or might be catastrophic. And somewhere in his locked memory was the key to everything.

Silva looked up at the dome, at Saturn's vast presence beyond, and wondered what he would do next. The only thing he knew for certain was that he had to find out the truth—about himself, about Dixon, about everything.

And he had to do it before those weapons were unloaded and Titan Station exploded into violence.
